kurz: Why a loss and a gain of the same size do not cancel each other out, and what this asymmetry means for volatility and leverage.

bloecke.md:
A portfolio loses 30% in one year and gains 30% the next. The average of the two years is zero, yet afterwards the portfolio stands at 91% of its starting value. This is because the two percentages refer to different amounts. The loss is deducted from the full capital, while the gain is added to the reduced remainder.

After minus 30%, €10,000 becomes €7,000. For this to become €10,000 again, €3,000 has to be earned on a base of €7,000, which is 42.9%. With small losses, this gap between the loss and the necessary recovery is small; with large losses, it grows sharply.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula indicates by what percentage the remaining capital has to grow to get back to its previous level. With every percentage point of loss, the denominator becomes smaller, which is why the result rises faster and faster as the loss grows.
variablen: loss as a decimal, e.g. 0.5 for minus 50%
bloecke.beispiel: v = 0.5: 1 / 0.5 - 1 = 1.00, that is, plus 100%. The remaining half has to double.

bloecke.titel: Required gain and recovery time after a loss

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using 1/(1-v)-1. Up to minus 30%, the required gain rises moderately, and after that ever more steeply.

bloecke.md: The loss is measured against the original capital, the recovery against the smaller remainder. Equal percentages for loss and gain therefore do not offset each other. Mathematically, every percentage point of loss avoided is worth more than an additional percentage point of gain.

## Average return and final wealth

This asymmetry does not only take effect after a crash. It is present in every series of returns, including a predominantly positive one. Two portfolios with the same annual average reach different final values as soon as one of them fluctuates, and the fluctuating portfolio always comes off worse.

Both portfolios start with €10,000 and run for 20 years.

- Portfolio A achieves exactly plus 8% every year.
- Portfolio B alternately achieves plus 28% and minus 12%. Its arithmetic average is also 8%.

At the end, portfolio A stands at €46,610 and portfolio B at €32,880. The difference of €13,730 arises solely from the fluctuation. Portfolio B effectively grows by 6.13% a year, even though its annual returns average 8%.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula is an approximation of the reduction by which fluctuation lowers growth compared with the average return. It is called volatility drag or variance drain. The higher the fluctuation, the less accurate the approximation becomes.
variablen: actual annual growth of the capital
standard deviation of the annual returns as a decimal
bloecke.beispiel: Portfolio B: sigma = 0.20, so 8% - 0.20^2/2 = 8% - 2.0% = 6.0%. The exact growth is 6.13%, so the approximation is 0.13 percentage points off.

bloecke.md: The formula can be checked against real index series. In each of the four following cases, over periods of 25 to 56 years, it matches the measured gap between average and growth to within a few tenths of a percentage point.

bloecke.titel: Average return and growth of capital
bloecke.unter: The gap between the two bars is caused by fluctuation and is largest for the DAX and for emerging markets.

bloecke.titel: Testing the approximation with index data

bloecke.md:
Two things follow from this. First, the drag depends solely on fluctuation and is not a matter of chance. If fluctuation halves, the drag falls to a quarter. Second, the quality of an investment does not depend only on the average return. A fund with a 10% average and 30% volatility grows by around 5.5% a year, a fund with an 8% average and 12% volatility by around 7.3%.

## Recovery in real index series

bloecke.titel: Performance of €100 invested at the end of 1999
bloecke.unter: The world index only regained the starting value of 100 at the end of 2013. The DAX was briefly above it at the end of 2007 and immediately fell below it again afterwards.

bloecke.md:
Calculated net in euros, the MSCI World lost a cumulative 44.7% from the end of 1999 to the end of 2002. A gain of 80.9%, not 44.7%, was therefore needed to return to the starting value. This gain was only achieved in 2013, after fourteen calendar years. Over the same period, the DAX fell by 58.4% and therefore needed plus 140.5%. At the end of 2007, it was back above the starting value for a few months and immediately fell below it again in 2008. It only stayed above the starting value permanently from 2012 onwards.

Both series are index levels without costs and without taxes. A real portfolio with custody fees, spreads and fund charges would have taken one to two years longer in each case. Investors who kept paying in monthly during this period were in profit much earlier, because their new contributions were invested at low prices. The arithmetic of recovery applies to an amount invested once and not to a savings plan.

## Leverage and volatility drag

Because the drag grows with the square of the fluctuation, it also grows with the square of the leverage. A product with 2x leverage doubles the expected return but quadruples the drag. In addition, there are the costs of the borrowed money. The borrowed portion is financed at the money market rate plus a margin, so currently at a rate above the ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% (in force since 16 September 2026).

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation of leverage on an index with an 8% average and 18% volatility

bloecke.md: The table is an illustrative calculation with assumed financing costs of 3.5% per borrowed unit and not a forecast. The pattern it shows is robust, however. At first, growth barely rises with leverage, reaches its maximum in this example at leverage of around 1.4 and falls thereafter. From leverage of 4 upwards, the capital shrinks, even though the underlying index is rising. Fluctuation multiplies directly with leverage, whereas the return only appears to, because volatility drag and financing costs are deducted from it.

bloecke.titel: Path dependency of a 2x product with an unchanged index
bloecke.unter: Worked example without market data. The index swings between 100 and 110, while the product, reset to 2x leverage every day, loses 5.4%.

bloecke.md:
Leveraged ETFs and **factor certificates** reset their leverage to the target value every trading day. The stated factor therefore only applies for one day. Over weeks, the price path determines the result, and in a volatile sideways market the product loses money even if the underlying ends up unchanged. This loss is neither a fee nor a mistake by the issuer. It follows from the [[Path dependency|path dependency]] of the daily adjustment.

With **knock-out certificates**, the arithmetic of recovery no longer applies at all. If the barrier is touched, the certificate expires, even if this happens overnight or only for a second. No percentage gain leads back from zero, because the formula 1/(1-v) has no value at v = 1. Since 2018, fixed leverage limits for retail clients have applied to CFDs in the EU (30:1 on major currency pairs, 20:1 on major indices, 5:1 on individual shares, 2:1 on crypto assets), together with negative balance protection. This protection rules out an obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht), but not a total loss.

Because the drag depends on the square of the fluctuation, any measure that reduces fluctuation without reducing the average return is mathematically a source of additional return. The best-known case is diversification across countries and asset classes. Two portfolios with a 9% average and 12% and 24% volatility respectively reach around €73,100 and €44,200 after 25 years for every €10,000 invested. Conversely, avoiding the very large crashes is worth more than achieving additional return in good years, but only if the avoidance costs nothing. A hedge that permanently costs return replaces a possible loss with a certain one.

In exact terms, `ln(1 + r_geo)`, the logarithm of the geometric growth factor, equals the average of the logarithms of the annual growth factors `ln(1 + r)`. The formula `r_geo = r_arith - sigma^2/2` follows from the series expansion of the logarithm and holds exactly only in the limiting case of continuous, lognormally distributed returns.

In practice, with annual volatility of up to about 25%, it is usually off by less than half a percentage point (see table above). With very large individual moves, the higher-order terms of the series are no longer negligible. If the series contains a gain of 100%, the formula overestimates the drag; if it contains a loss of 60%, it underestimates it. For leveraged products with a factor of 3 or 4, it is therefore only an indication of direction, and the result there is usually worse than the formula suggests.

mitnehmen: After a loss v, a gain of 1/(1-v)-1 is needed to recover: after minus 20%, plus 25%; after minus 50, plus 100; after minus 80, plus 400.
The average of the annual returns is always higher than the annual growth of the capital, and the gap of approximately sigma^2/2 is confirmed by real indices.
Fluctuation is not only unpleasant, it also directly reduces the return, and with half the fluctuation the drag falls to a quarter.
Leverage k doubles or triples the return linearly, but the volatility drag quadratically, so that beyond a certain point the result falls despite rising leverage.
After a slump of 44.7%, the MSCI World in euros needed fourteen calendar years to get back to its old level, and recovery times of this order of magnitude must be expected.

begriffe.text: The gain that the remaining capital has to achieve after a loss to get back to its previous level: 1/(1-v)-1. After minus 50%, that is plus 100%.
The gap between the average of the annual returns and the annual growth of the capital. It is approximately sigma^2/2 and therefore depends solely on fluctuation.

The property of a product whose result depends on the path of the underlying between its starting and final levels and not solely on these two levels. Typical of leveraged products that are rebalanced daily.

A debt security that multiplies the daily percentage change of an underlying by a constant factor. Because of the daily recalculation, it is path-dependent; in addition, there are financing costs and issuer risk.
